EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong surface low associated with an upper level trough in the Gulf of Alaska increased snowfall over Southcentral Alaska on January 5th as flow shifted southwesterly. The trough was negatively tilted, which further aided in providing lift for additional snowfall. In addition, the low created a very tight pressure gradient over Kachemak Bay and the southern Kenai Peninsula January 6, 2026. In addition to the pressure gradient, heavy snow developed over Kachemak Bay producing heavy snow and blowing snow over the region. Strong Westerly winds also produced high surf along the Homer Spit.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Most areas of Anchorage received 12 to 18 inches of snow between January 4 and January 6 via storm reports. Snowfall across town was first concentrated on the west side before shifting eastward as a second round of snowfall arrived the night of January 5.  This second round also had higher snow ratios due to a very cold air mass pushing in, allowing for ratios of 25:1 and even 30:1 in some spots. Another influence from the cold air was the creation of a deep dendritic growth layer from sea level to 15kft. Snowfall at the Anchorage airport started after 10:00 PM January 4 and lasted through 6:00 PM of January 6th. There were periods of moderate to heavy snowfall during this time.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A complex upper low over the Canadian Archipelago allowed several disturbances to rotate southwards towards Alaska's Arctic coastline during the second week of March, 2026. During this time frame a classic barrier jet set up along the NE Arctic Coast from Point Thomson to Barter Island resulting in gusty WSW winds, blowing snow, and blizzard conditions for the region.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Winds began to increase rapidly from the west and southwest along the NE Arctic coastline during the early morning hours of March 10th. By mid morning blizzard conditions were being reported by the Point Thomson AWOS (PAAD) with wind speeds sustained at around 35 mph and gusts exceeding 40 mph. This resulted in blowing snow reducing the visibility to or below 1/4 mile for a little over 13 hours before conditions improved. A max wind gusts of 47 mph was registered shortly after midday.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The third in a series of blizzards to affect the NE Arctic coastline unfolded to start the third week of March. Disturbances rotating southwards from a stagnant upper low over the Canadian Arctic once again produced a barrier jet that brought strong westerly flow and significant blowing snow to locations from Niuqsut to Barter Island.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: For the second time in less than a week winds began to increase rapidly from the west and southwest across the Eastern Arctic coastline in response to a storm system anchored high in the Arctic. By mid morning on the 16th the Point Thomson AWOS (PAAD) was reporting blizzard conditions with sustained winds of 35 to 40 mph and gusts of 45 mph or higher. The visibility dropped to 1/4 mile or lower due to blowing snow created by these strong winds. These conditions would persist for close to 36 hours before conditions began to improve. At the storms peak, wind gusts were measured at 50 mph or greater.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Heading into the third weekend of March, yet another strong disturbance approached Alaska's Arctic coastline from the north. And as a result, blizzard conditions developed across portions of the NE Arctic coast for the forth time in a span of only 3 weeks. This time the swath of stronger westerly winds expanded to include areas from Deadhorse all the way east to Barter Island and beyond.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The areas fourth blizzard in less than three weeks began to unfold during the late morning hours of March 20th. Winds at the Point Thomson AWOS (PAAD) topped 35 mph kicking up plenty of blowable snow and reducing the visibility to 1/4 mile. The winds would stay elevated at 35 mph with gusts to 45 mph for more than 15 hours along with visibility readings of 1/4 mile of less well into the nighttime hours. While the wind speeds remained elevated into the overnight hours, the visibility began to improve prior to dawn the next day.

EVENT_NARRATIVE: Strong west and southwest winds that had been confined to the Eastern Arctic coast began to spread further west along the central Beaufort Sea coast during the late morning hours of March 20th. A little after midday, the Deadhorse ASOS (PASC) began indicating sustained winds of 30 mph with gusts to 35 mph or higher. These winds lofted snow and the blowing snow dropped the visibility to around 1/4 mile. Conditions were made worse by ice fog that also developed across the region. These blizzard conditions persisted about 8 hours before the blowing snow and winds subsided enough to allow for improvements in the visibility.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A developing 970 mb low over the north west Gulf of Alaska, sent an occluded front into the panhandle with the associated triple point tracking over the northern inner channels the afternoon and evening of March 6th. This caused winds through the inner channels to increase out of the south, reaching high wind criteria in Skagway until after the low center jumped into the Yukon and weakened. The following day, another low tracked in but was slightly further south and Skagway saw peak gusts just below warning criteria.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The Marine Exchange of Alaska observation at the Skagway Ore Dock measured the first high wind gust as winds shifted suddenly out of the south with a peak of 56.4kt (65mph) at 230pm on the 6th. The Skagway Airport ASOS measured a peak gust of 55kt (63mph) at 415pm and the Marine Exchange station at the harbor measured a peak gust of 51.8kt (60mph) at 714pm. High wind gusts continued into the night at the Airport until 1104pm and at the Ore Dock until 123am.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A nearly stationary low pressure center in the Eastern Gulf of Alaska continued to send scattered snow showers over portions of Prince of Wales Island on the 10th with some becoming heavy at times. During the overnight period and into the morning of the 11th, the snow showers became more persistent with greater accumulations over the SW portion of the island.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A trained spotter in Craig, on the SW side of Prince of Wales Island, measured 5 inches of snow between 8pm on the 10th to 133am on the 11th and another 2 inches by 343am AKDT. The COOP observer in Craig measured a 24hr total of 11 inches at 845am AKDT with moderate snow showers continuing and another 3.2 inches the following morning. The COOP in Klawock measured 9 inches of new snow at 9am AKST while the COOP in Thorne Bay on the eastern side of the island only measured 2.5 inches.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Bands of snow showers fell across the region for multiple days with largely advisory level rates, but with some became more organized and trained in areas for a longer period of time, such as Pelican on the 18th into the 19th.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A spotter in Pelican reported around 10 inches of snow had fallen on the 18th and another 2 inches overnight into the morning of the 19th for an estimated 12 inches in a 24 hour period. Timing of the snowfall start/stop times based on other nearby observation stations.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Low pressure lingered over the eastern Gulf over the first couple days of March causing multiple days of accumulating snow across the panhandle. Most places saw advisory level rates with some periods nearing warning level rates. As the low center tracked east across the central panhandle on the 4th, cold temperatures and northerly winds caused heavy snow to stack up over the Haines area. This was followed quickly by a warm front on the 5th which continued snow to accumulate in Haines through the evening while other parts of the region had transitioned to rain.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A trained spotter in Gustavus reported periods of snow through the 4th, but with snowfall rates increasing at 8pm in the evening and a new snow accumulation of 6.5 inches falling during the overnight period to 730am on the 5th. Moderate to heavy snow fell through the morning of the 5th with mixing then a change over to rain in town by around 1pm and around 3pm at the Glacier Bay National Park. Snowfall accumulations at the park were missing for the morning of the 5th but with a snow depth increase of 13 inches and heavy snow falling at the time.

By 8am on the 5th, the same location had a new 24hr total of 12.9 inches of snow with snow continuing to fall. The COOP in town, at a lower elevation, measured a 24hr snowfall of 8.9 inches. Snow tapered off through the evening of the 5th as temperatures warmed and new snowfall measurements the following morning were just over 5 inches with a glaze of freezing rain. The COOP station at Haines Customs reported considerably less snow during this period with less than 2 inches each day.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Snow showers incoming from the Gulf produced wildly differing snowfall amounts across Juneau area. Amounts ranged from 1 inch at Tee Harbor to just over a foot from Lemon Creek to Douglas Island.

By 5am AKDT on the 9th, a report on North Douglas had at least 8 inches of snow in the previous 12 hours. An NWS employee in the same area measured 12 inches of accumulation between 9pm and 6am AKDT. A report from the Lemon Creek area also had nearly 12 inches by 745am AKDT. Snow showers continued through mid day on the 9th, then rates decreased. Other parts of the Juneau zone, particularly north of the airport had much lighter snowfall accumulations from these showers reaching just over 4 inches at the NWS Office and less than 2 inches at Lena Point.

Intermittent snow showers occurred from Yakutat to Sitka, but showers moved out of Sitka and Pelican/Elfin Cove while rates picked up at Yakutat through the early morning hours of Sunday the 15th. A winter weather advisory was upgraded to a warning as visibility dropped to a quarter mile.

Visibility periodically fell to a quarter mile through the morning with around 7 inches of snowfall accumulation measured by 1pm when snow let up.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A low pressure tracked northward across the panhandle starting the morning of Sunday the 15th and continuing through Monday. Steady snowfall fell across the area, with strong winds and a change over to rain across the far south in the evening, and heaviest rates in Hyder and portions of the northern panhandle.

The wind was already picking up at the airport in the morning with gusts of 20-30mph. Theses gusts continued to increase through the day while snow continued. Other wind gusts with this system across Ketchikan ranged from 40-56mph.  A social media report from 7 mile South Tongass Highway noted 6.5 inches of heavy and wet snow had fallen. A trained spotter near downtown Ketchikan reported 6.5 inches of snow as well by 6pm AKDT and the airport reported a change to rain shortly after this. The COOP at the northern end of town saw only 1.8 inches of snow and was already mixing at their 3pm report time.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong low pressure system made its way into the Bering Sea early Wednesday morning (4/22), bringing widespread snow, mixed precipitation, and strong winds to Western Alaska and portions of the Western/Central Interior. As the low moved inland, a front moving northeast off the low brought predominantly snow to the Seward Peninsula and YK Delta with 2 to 8 of total accumulations. This system was able to support gusty winds up to 60 mph and easily created widespread blowing snow conditions to much of the West Coast. By the time the front made its way into the Interior, a rain/snow mix of around 2 to 6 fell in addition to strong southerly gap winds through both Isabel and Windy Pass. Winds gusted anywhere between 65 to 75 mph through the passes, creating difficult travel conditions along the Parks and Richardson Highway. Effects from this system subsequently diminished by the weekend (4/25 through 4/26), resulting in a steady warming trend as upper level southerly flow set up over the area.

Conditions were at their lowest between 14:00L on 2/19 to 17:00L on 2/19 due to snow squalls in the area.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The 2026 spring breakup along the Yukon River was highly dynamic, defined by a combination of thermal ice decay and severe mechanical ice jams. Because of an exceptionally cold winter and a cool spring, the river ice was thicker than normal and had not deteriorated significantly before the main breakup front arrived. Early-season flooding was driven by localized snowmelt and ice jams on independent river systems and upper sections of the Yukon River.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The local Emergency Manager reported that rapid snowmelt caused poor drainage areas to overflow, leading to imminent flooding of low-lying and flood-prone locations. The most severe flooding occurred near Fish Creek, requiring ongoing rescue operations as several homes took on water and had to be evacuated.

Public and emergency mangers reported flooding in Chalkyiksik, with low-lying and poor drainage areas experiencing most of the flooding. By Saturday May 9th, the ice jam had broken up downriver and conditions had improved.

The Emmonak High School had to be opened as an emergency shelter for displaced residents.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong low pressure system entered the Bering Sea to start the month of May. With a cold Arctic high pressure system over the Beaufort Sea, strong south and southwesterly winds developed from Alaska's West Coast eastwards toward the Alaska Range. Along the West Coast, the winds combined with light to moderate snow to create blizzard conditions, while the Alaska Range passes saw damaging wind gusts to start the month.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The Point Lay AWOS (PPIZ) reported just shy of 12 hours of blizzard conditions with wind gusts as high as 39 mph and visibility levels dropping to or just below 1/4 mile in blowing snow.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A series of shortwave troughs lifted northward through the Gulf of Alaska into the Northern Gulf Coast on May 1. Winds gusted over 75 mph at times until 8:00 PM the same day. A couple who lives on the Hillside said that their weather station measured 121 mph winds. They also mentioned that some members of their community had damage to their deck, roofs, and trailers.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A North Pacific low moved into the Bering on May 14. The low lifted northward on May 15, with its front sweeping eastward across the Alaska Peninsula. This tightened pressure gradients and increased wind speeds, especially through bays and passes. Cold Bay experienced a period of gusty winds on May 15 before the weakening low lifted further north.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The Cold Bay ASOS (PACD) observed winds gusting over 75 mph starting 12:05 PM AKDT May 15. Winds frequently gusted over 75 mph, with a peak wind gust of 83 mph at 12:59 PM, until 1:33 PM, when wind gusts dropped below 70 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An atmospheric river brought snow followed by high winds, warming temperatures and heavy rain to the panhandle January 8th and 9th. A low pressure center developed along a triple point front as it tracked NE across the western Gulf of Alaska on the 9th. The low center deepened to 960mb as it approached the northern Gulf and the frontal system brought a period of high winds to the central and southern panhandle. This system brought with it heavy snow across the north, followed by a significant warm-up, heavy rain, localized flooding due to previous heavy snow blocking drainages, and avalanches. The flooding falls into the advisory level, but the rain was an additional impact due to the added weight of the snow on structures. Disaster declarations were expanded to more communities across the northern panhandle after this storm.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Intermittent light snow fell on the 8th, becoming steady late with winds turning out of the north. Visibility fell to a half mile in the 6am hour on the 9th at the airport. A trained spotter measured 5.8 inches of snow by 7am out the road near Cohen Drive and another spotter measured 7.5 inches just before 8am. The Juneau Airport began mixing with rain around 8am while temperatures were still 30F, then fully transitioned to rain over the next 2 hours. The DOT RWIS station near Cohen Drive continued to see snow or a mix into the afternoon, then temperatures warmed above 32F at 5pm. Freezing levels rose steadily through the event, rising to around 4kft by 6pm based on the South Douglas JAWS profiler.||During the evening of the 8th, the City and Borough of Juneau announced public facilities and schools would be closed the following day due to ongoing hazardous road and weather conditions. Several small avalanches were reported during the the 9th off of Mt. Juneau, Mt. Roberts and the Thane area. No damage was reported from the avalanches and evacuation advisories and road closures were already in place. As rain fell on deep snowpack, localized flooding reports came in through the evening of the 9th particularly in Douglas, downtown Juneau, along Egan Drive, and in the Mendenhall Valley. The additional weight of snow and rain caused a vessel to sink in Douglas Harbor. This was the 11th vessel to sink in Juneau since the December record snow began. Other small out buildings and sheds succumbed to the added weight of rain on snow as well. A disaster declaration was in effect during this time.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: After an active period of multiple systems moving through the area bringing periods of high winds to the southern panhandle, a stronger system arrived bringing high winds to majority of the Panhandle on the 13th into the 14th. This low center tracked northward through the eastern gulf, while deepening, along with a storm force front. The low center moved onshore along the NE Gulf Coast in vicinity of Yakutat overnight Tuesday the 13th. As the low jumped inland, winds spiked up through the inner channels, lasting longest for the Skagway area.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Strong easterly winds with gusts of 45-55mph across the Yakutat area late on the 13th, saw a sharp wind shift out of the west in the 1am hour, spiking up to high wind. The peak wind gust measured at the Yakutat Airport ASOS was 53kt (61mph) at 248am on the 14th.

The Juneau airport ASOS measured a peak gust of 47kt (54mph) at 1056pm. The Marine Exchange station at the AML dock downtown measured a peak gust of 50kt (58mph) at 1155pm. Also in the 10 and 11pm hours, other nearby stations at elevation topped out at 88mph at the Tram and 82mph at Eaglecrest.||The City and Borough of Juneau continued with an avalanche advisory during this time and DOT had Thane Road closed due to the high avalanche danger.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Temperatures cooled across SE Alaska along with outflow winds during the first couple days of January after December's big snow dump. This allowed the next system that moved in from the west on the 4th and 5th to start out as snow. Prefrontal snow showers during the evening of the 4th added to the storm total snow for parts of the northern and central panhandle, then the main system moved in overnight with heavy snow on Monday the 5th (set to be the first day back at school after Winter Break for most locations). The southern panhandle saw a change over to rain during the day on the 5th, then the rain/snow line pushed northward through the night and into the morning of the 6th. Some strong winds accompanied the front, starting out of the north then shifting to the south with the front and causing temperatures to rise.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Light, dry, fluffy snow fell during the afternoon and evening of the 4th based on spotter reports with over 5 inches of accumulation already by 8pm. The COOP at the Glacier Bay National Park measured 9.5 inches of new snow at their 8am observation on the 5th. Other trained spotters in town measured 6-8.5 inches that morning. Snow continued into the afternoon with variable rates reported including 6.5 inches between 930am and 345pm and a total of 13.5 inches by 7pm when a transition to rain was noted. The Gustavus Airport AWOS was down during this time, but other stations in the area saw periodic wind gusts of around 20mph during this time.||After significant snowfall in December and this additional snow, plus a transition to rain adding to the weight, damage to roofs and outbuildings likely occurred, but none were reported to the NWS.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A deep upper-level low over the Eastern Arctic tracked southwest toward the Bering Strait during the last week of January. This system pushed a cold front across the region, producing very strong winds along and immediately behind the boundary. These winds triggered initial blizzard conditions along the Northwest Arctic coast, which then spread westward toward the western Seward Peninsula.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A long duration blizzard set in along the central Arctic coastline during the morning hours of the 27th. The Deadhorse ASOS (PASC) reported persistent wind gusts of 40 to 50 mph for almost two full days, resulting in blowing snow and visibility readings at or below 1/4 mile. The winds eventually subsided enough after 45 hours to allow for a gradual improvement in the visibility.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The second week of February saw the first of 3 back to back major winter storms move across Alaska's West Coast and Interior. The week began with abnormally cold readings across the all of Northern and Central Alaska. By Monday a very strong storm system entered the Bering Sea and proceeded to move northeastward across the West Coast and the Interior of Alaska over the next several days. Initially the storm brought heavy snow and strong winds from the Bering Strait coastline down to the Yukon Delta region which resulted in blizzard conditions. As the storm moved deeper into the Interior the storm produced heavy snowfall and occasional snow squalls.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Snow began along the Western Arctic Coast shortly after midnight on the 11th. By mid morning on the 12th strong winds and heavy snow had brought the visibility down to around 1/4 mile at the Point Lay AWOS (PPIZ), resulting in near blizzard conditions with winds sustained around 30 mph. The visibility dropped further as winds climbed to above 35 mph shortly before midnight. Blizzard conditions continued for approximately 30 hours at Point Lay as winds gusted to between 40 and 50 mph resulting in considerable blowing snow.

Disaster declarations were expanded to more communities across the northern panhandle after this storm.

The Sitka AML dock measured a peak gust of 50.2kt (58mph) at 551pm.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A front atop a ridge in the East Bering moved into the Southwest Alaska Mainland, bringing a swath of precipitation and gusty southerly winds. The southerly winds brought about warm air advection, causing temperatures to increase. However, before temperatures rose above freezing in the Kuskokwim Delta, the gusty winds with the front allowed for a period of blizzard conditions in the Kuskokwim Delta Coast on February 13.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An upper level Arctic trough dug through Southcentral Alaska and into the Gulf starting February 19. This caused Arctic air to surge through Southcentral into the Gulf while pressure gradients tightened between a strong ridge in the Bering and a surface low that developed in the Northeast Gulf. These factors led to widespread gusty gap winds in Prince William Sound and Kodiak Island. In addition, the thermal and pressure gradients between the Matanuska Valley and the Copper River Basin strengthened enough to allow for strong, gusty northeast winds in the Matanuska Valley.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Temperatures cooled across SE Alaska along with outflow winds during the first couple days of January after December's big snow dump. This allowed the next system that moved in from the west on the 4th and 5th to start out as snow. Prefrontal snow showers during the evening of the 4th added to the storm total snow for parts of the northern and central panhandle, then the main system moved in overnight with heavy snow on Monday the 5th (set to be the first day back at school after Winter Break for most locations). The southern panhandle saw a change over to rain during the day on the 5th, then the rain/snow line pushed northward through the night and into the morning of the 6th. Some strong winds accompanied the front, starting out of the north then shifting to the south with the front and causing temperatures to rise.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Light snow began to fall in the Petersburg area shortly after midnight with rates increasing through the early morning hours of the 5th. Visibility fell to a quarter mile in the 9am hour and a social media comment reported that 6 inches of snow had already fallen by 10am. Snow continued through the day, with some reports of mixing, then rates let up in the evening. A social media report near Scow Bay already had 9.5 inches of snow by 6pm. The COOP station at the Petersburg Airport measured 9.5 inches of new snow at their 10pm report. The airport AWOS saw a change to rain shortly after this measurement.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The second week of February saw the first of 3 back to back major winter storms move across Alaska's West Coast and Interior. The week began with abnormally cold readings across the all of Northern and Central Alaska. By Monday a very strong storm system entered the Bering Sea and proceeded to move northeastward across the West Coast and the Interior of Alaska over the next several days. Initially the storm brought heavy snow and strong winds from the Bering Strait coastline down to the Yukon Delta region which resulted in blizzard conditions. As the storm moved deeper into the Interior the storm produced heavy snowfall and occasional snow squalls.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Strong northeast winds and heavy snow arrived at St Lawrence Island early on the 13th and continued throughout the day and into the wee hours of the next morning. By early afternoon the Gambell AWOS (PAGM) was reporting wind gusts of 40 to 50 mph and a visibility at or below 1/4 mile due to blowing snow. These blizzard conditions continued into the evening hours with strong winds continuing to produce near blizzard conditions well into the overnight hours before the winds finally weakened a bit.

Prefrontal snow showers during the evening of the 4th added to the storm total snow for parts of the northern and central panhandle, then the main system moved in overnight with heavy snow on Monday the 5th (set to be the first day back at school after Winter Break for most locations). The southern panhandle saw a change over to rain during the day on the 5th, then the rain/snow line pushed northward through the night and into the morning of the 6th. Some strong winds accompanied the front, starting out of the north then shifting to the south with the front and causing temperatures to rise.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Light snow began to fall in the Yakutat area during the evening of the 4th with rates picking up after midnight. Visibility fell to a quarter mile at times through the morning of the 5th with sustained E-NE winds increasing to 20mph. An NWS Employee measured 9.2 inches of snow at 920am and another 2.6 inches 4 hours later. As temperatures steadily rose through the day, a period of freezing rain was observed at the airport in the evening followed by a wind shift to the SW and a change to rain for a short period of time.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An upper level Arctic trough dug through Southcentral Alaska and into the Gulf starting February 19. This caused Arctic air to surge through Southcentral into the Gulf while pressure gradients tightened between a strong ridge in the Bering and a surface low that developed in the Northeast Gulf. These factors led to widespread gusty gap winds in Prince William Sound and Kodiak Island. In addition, the thermal and pressure gradients between the Matanuska Valley and the Copper River Basin strengthened enough to allow for strong, gusty northeast winds in the Matanuska Valley.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The Kodiak Gull Island Marine observation site recorded wind gusts over 70 mph starting 7:42 PM AKST February 19. The strongest gust recorded from the site was 89 mph at 9:32 PM the same day. The Kodiak Airport ASOS (PADQ) saw winds gusting over 70 mph at 8:03 PM and 8:11 PM before winds decreased in strength by 10:00 PM. A second, stronger round of gusty winds started at 11:40 PM with a 73 mph gust. The airport officially hit criteria of 75 mph at 12:53 AM AKST February 20. Winds frequently gusted over 70 mph until after 4:00 AM AKST February 20.||Kenneth Folsom, an Emergency Manager in Kodiak, reported that a roof was blown off somewhere in Kodiak City.

EVENT_NARRATIVE: Light snow was falling in Hyder during the morning of the 5th with drifting noted by a spotter at 8am. By late morning 2.5 inches had accumulated, then rates increased as indicated by the METAR in the neighboring town of Stewart B.C., dropping below a quarter mile for several hours in the afternoon. By 320pm AKST new snow accumulation in Hyder had reached over 6 inches in just the previous 4 hours. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A low pressure system in the southern Bering Sea moved northeast over the Aleutian Islands bringing widespread snow showers and gusty north/northeast winds to much of southeast Alaska and parts of the Western Interior. The front on the leading edge of the Bering Sea low initiated the first waves of snowfall in the southeast Interior, while gusty north/northeast winds strengthened on the western side of the low. Falling snow and gusty winds created long-lasting blizzard conditions to coastal areas along the Lower Yukon. The strongest winds settled over St. Lawrence Island and along the Norton Sound coastline as the low moved further inland.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The Gambell AWOS (PAGM) site first met high wind criteria on 1/5/26 at 04:42L reporting 49 mph sustained winds, gusting at 59 mph. The AWOS site reported a peak observation at 04:56L on 1/5/26 of sustained winds at 47 mph, gusting to 63 mph. Wind gusts were in the upper 50 mph range for over 10 hrs as of 15:00L on 1/5/26.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A low pressure system in the Gulf of Alaska pushed a strong frontal boundary northward into central Alaska bringing widespread snowfall and blizzard conditions. Winds strengthened ahead of the front, producing gusty winds through Alaska Range Passes and Dalton Highway Summits. Snowfall moved through the Interior from southeast to northwest, with the highest accumulations across the Alaska Range. Blizzard conditions developed in areas where falling snow and gusty winds were present. Effects from this storm were seen as far south as the Alaska Range, to as far north as the central/eastern Brooks Range.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A Vitus (Energy Company) employee reported whiteout conditions with drifting and blowing snow at 07:58L on 1/11/26. They also estimated approximately 8 inches of snow had fallen, but couldn't verify because of the on-going blowing snow conditions. A DOT report at 07:53L on 1/11/26 later estimated as much as 12 inches of snow had fallen in and around Cantwell, with heavy blowing/drifting snow and gusty winds.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A 962mb low pressure system tracked northward into the central Gulf of Alaska through January 28th. An occluded front extending out to the east from the low brought a period of high winds across Annette Island.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The weather station at the Annette Island Packing Company measured high winds during the afternoon of the 28th between 1235pm and 4pm AKST. The peak gusts of 68mph occurred at 1245 and 1250pm.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The second week of February saw the first of 3 back to back major winter storms move across Alaska's West Coast and Interior. The week began with abnormally cold readings across the all of Northern and Central Alaska. By Monday a very strong storm system entered the Bering Sea and proceeded to move northeastward across the West Coast and the Interior of Alaska over the next several days. Initially the storm brought heavy snow and strong winds from the Bering Strait coastline down to the Yukon Delta region which resulted in blizzard conditions. As the storm moved deeper into the Interior the storm produced heavy snowfall and occasional snow squalls.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The COOP observer for Minchumina (LMHA2) reported a 24 snow total of 7.4 on the morning of the 15th. There was additional snowfall that fell outside this 24 hour window resulting in a storm total snowfall of 9.5. This data was supported by observations from the Minchumina AWOS (PAMH) which showed near constant light to moderate snowfall for almost 36 hours extending from the morning of the 14th through the afternoon of the 15th.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The first week of February 2026 saw an extensive cold trough aloft situated over the northern half of Alaska. Underneath this trough ambient temperatures hovered around -40 F for several days. Meanwhile across the North Slope and throughout the Brooks Range winds occasionally picked up, resulting in dangerous wind chill readings.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Just prior to midnight on the 8th, the Umiat Airfield RAWS (UMTA2) reported a wind chill value of -70 F as the air temperature dropped to -49 F and a west wind of 7 to 10 mph developed. These conditions persisted for close to 24 hours with the wind chill dropping to -70 F on several occasions.

The Chevak AWOS (PAVA) began reporting wind gusts in excess of 35 mph and visibilities as low as 1/4 mile shortly after 6am with full on blizzard conditions in place a few hours later. Meanwhile along the immediate coast the Hooper Bay AWOS (PAHP) was reporting similar conditions.
